summaries.example: Imagine your class is trying to decide whether a strange sound came from the hallway or the playground. Two groups give equally strong reasons. Instead of pretending to know which group is right, you might say, “I am not ready to choose.” This is like suspending judgment. Skeptics use this attitude when philosophers disagree about very deep questions.
summaries.summary: This entry tells the story of philosophical skepticism in Latin America. Skepticism is a careful way of investigating questions. A skeptic may find that different philosophical ideas have strong arguments on both sides, so the skeptic pauses instead of claiming certainty. Ancient skepticism had two main forms, Pyrrhonism and Academic skepticism. It was rediscovered during the Renaissance and became important in modern philosophy. Latin American philosophers share this long history, but many of them have been especially open to taking skepticism seriously. Oswaldo Porchat in Brazil and Ezequiel de Olaso in Argentina helped begin major modern study of skepticism in the region. Porchat developed “neo-Pyrrhonism,” a newer form that separates everyday life and appearances from claims about the deepest nature of reality. Later scholars supported, changed, or criticized these ideas. They also studied science, language, disagreement, knowledge, politics, ancient philosophy, modern thinkers, and literature. The entry presents a selective history rather than a complete list of every scholar or country.
key_ideas: Skeptics investigate questions but do not automatically accept or reject a final answer.
Philosophers often disagree, and this disagreement can be a reason to pause judgment.
Skepticism has ancient roots and later influenced many modern philosophers.
In Latin America, scholars have studied old and new skepticism, and many have treated it as a serious possibility rather than just an enemy to defeat.
Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, and Colombia have been especially important places for this work, while interest also appears elsewhere in the region.
summaries.why_it_matters: Skepticism teaches us to notice how difficult some questions are and to listen carefully when reasons conflict. It does not simply mean refusing to think or refusing to use evidence. The Latin American story also shows that philosophy grows through discussion across countries, traditions, and generations. Studying these debates can help us become more careful about what we know, what merely seems true, and how we treat people who disagree.

important_terms.definition: A way of investigating questions by not deciding that a claim is true or false when the reasons do not settle the issue.
Waiting to say “yes” or “no” about a claim because the evidence has not decided it.
A person or thinker who accepts a philosophical theory as the final answer.
A long tradition of skepticism connected with Pyrrho, an ancient Greek philosopher. It examines opposing arguments and avoids firm philosophical commitments.

questions_to_think_about: When is it wise to wait before deciding?
Can people disagree and still learn from one another?
Is saying “I do not know yet” a weakness, a strength, or both?

summaries.example: Suppose two philosophers disagree about whether a scientific theory reveals reality exactly as it is or only helps us predict what happens. A neo-Pyrrhonist might use empirical evidence and scientific methods while refusing to claim that the theory describes reality’s ultimate nature. The philosopher can say how things appear and how well a theory works without adding a dogmatic metaphysical story.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys the development of philosophical skepticism in Latin America and places it within a wider history extending from ancient Greece to contemporary analytic philosophy. Skepticism is characterized by inquiry accompanied by suspension of judgment: unlike dogmatists, skeptics neither affirm nor deny a disputed philosophical proposition. The central challenge arises from conflict among philosophical doctrines and from the difficulty of finding a criterion that can decide between competing arguments without itself becoming part of the dispute. Ancient Pyrrhonism and Academic skepticism supplied distinct resources that were rediscovered in the Renaissance and used by modern philosophers. In Latin America, systematic work grew especially through Oswaldo Porchat in Brazil and Ezequiel de Olaso in Argentina. Porchat’s neo-Pyrrhonism treats skepticism as a coherent, general attitude. Its negative side emphasizes diaphonía and epokhé; its positive side describes phainómena and common life as what remains available after suspension of dogmatic theories. This position is not Cartesian skepticism: it does not require mentalism or solipsism, and it can accommodate ordinary life, empirical reasoning, and scientific results. The entry then reviews reactions to neo-Pyrrhonism, including scientific, realist, transcendental, political, rustic, and anti-skeptical approaches. It also surveys regional research on meaning skepticism, Wittgenstein, disagreement, ancient and modern skepticism, Kant, Hume, literature, and related philosophical traditions.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes skepticism from methodological doubt: neo-Pyrrhonism is presented as an articulated stance rather than merely a tool used to strengthen another theory.

Ancient skepticism included Pyrrhonism and Academic skepticism. Latin American historians have examined how both traditions shaped modern philosophy, including the work of Montaigne, Descartes, Bacon, Bayle, Hume, and Kant.
Porchat’s neo-Pyrrhonism begins with diaphonía, the unresolved conflict among philosophical views, and responds with epokhé.

Neo-Pyrrhonism distinguishes ordinary phenomena and common life from dogmatic claims about what things are ultimately like. It therefore need not reject ordinary knowledge, empirical inquiry, or scientific practice.

Latin American philosophers have proposed, defended, refined, and rejected skeptical positions. Their debates include science, truth, language and meaning, disagreement, self-knowledge, politics, and anti-skeptical strategies.

The regional scholarship is diverse and interconnected, but the entry is selective and notes that the relatively recent development of the field makes a fully balanced historical assessment difficult.
summaries.why_it_matters: The history presented here broadens the picture of where philosophical innovation occurs. Latin American scholars have not merely received European and Anglo-American debates; they have developed interpretations, distinctions, and new skeptical proposals of their own. The disputes also clarify a lasting philosophical question: how can inquiry proceed when our theories conflict and when the standards used to judge them are themselves contestable? Skepticism pressures epistemology, metaphysics, science, language, politics, and the history of philosophy to explain what counts as knowledge and what kinds of commitment inquiry requires.

important_terms.definition: Philosophical inquiry that withholds affirmation and denial when competing arguments do not establish a justified conclusion.
The skeptical practice of withholding judgment rather than endorsing or rejecting a disputed proposition.
A philosophical position that affirmatively commits to a theory or doctrine, especially about the ultimate nature of things.
An ancient skeptical tradition associated with Pyrrho and Sextus Empiricus, using opposing arguments to resist dogmatic conclusions.
A newer skeptical position developed by Oswaldo Porchat that treats skepticism as a general philosophical stance, not merely as a temporary method of doubt.
The conflict or disagreement among philosophical doctrines, especially when no neutral criterion settles the dispute.
What appears in experience or ordinary life; in neo-Pyrrhonism, it is distinguished from dogmatic claims about reality beyond appearances.
An argument strategy that seeks to answer skepticism by claiming that certain conditions must already hold for thought, knowledge, or argument to be possible.

questions_to_think_about: Does persistent philosophical disagreement justify suspension of judgment, or can a neutral standard resolve it?
Can someone use ordinary beliefs and scientific reasoning without making dogmatic claims about ultimate reality?
How might a skeptical view of meaning differ from skepticism about the external world?
Do transcendental arguments answer skepticism, or do they depend on assumptions the skeptic can question?
What might be gained, and what might be lost, by treating skepticism as a possible philosophical stance rather than a problem to eliminate?

summaries.example: Your friends are arguing about whether a rumor is true. One group has a convincing story, but another group has an equally convincing explanation. You might still act normally while saying, “I cannot decide yet.” Philosophers call this suspension of judgment. A skeptic does not have to stop learning; instead, the skeptic keeps examining the reasons without claiming that one final explanation has won.
summaries.summary: This entry explains how philosophical skepticism developed as a field of study in Latin America. A skeptic investigates a question but suspends judgment when competing philosophical positions cannot be fairly decided. This differs from dogmatism, which commits to a theory about how things really are. The tradition reaches back to ancient Pyrrhonism and Academic skepticism. After skepticism was rediscovered in the Renaissance, it influenced modern philosophers and became a continuing challenge for theories of knowledge and reality. In Latin America, the field grew especially through the work of Oswaldo Porchat of Brazil and Ezequiel de Olaso of Argentina. Porchat’s neo-Pyrrhonism is more than a temporary doubt. It is a general philosophical position with a negative side, which uses disagreement and opposing arguments to support suspension of judgment, and a positive side, which describes ordinary life and appearances without claiming to reveal ultimate reality. This view can still allow everyday action, empirical investigation, and scientific reasoning. Other Latin American philosophers have criticized or revised it. Some argue that science, truth, or ordinary language requires stronger commitments; others develop more radical versions of skepticism. Researchers across Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, Colombia, and other countries have also studied ancient skepticism, modern thinkers such as Descartes, Hume, and Kant, contemporary debates about language and knowledge, and connections with literature. The entry is a selective overview of a growing and varied field.
key_ideas: Skepticism is an activity of inquiry, not simply being suspicious of every everyday fact.
Ancient skepticism had two important forms: Pyrrhonism and Academic skepticism.
Skeptical arguments often begin with disagreement and ask whether any fair standard can settle the dispute.
Latin American philosophers have often treated skepticism as a serious, possibly defensible position, even when they reject it themselves.
Oswaldo Porchat’s neo-Pyrrhonism separates descriptions of how things appear from dogmatic claims about their ultimate nature.
The region’s scholarship includes work on science, knowledge, language, disagreement, politics, ancient philosophy, modern philosophy, and literature.
summaries.why_it_matters: Skepticism helps us understand why philosophers disagree and why being careful about certainty can be intellectually valuable. The Latin American history shows that skepticism is not one single opinion: scholars interpret it differently, apply it to science and language, or argue against it. Learning about these disagreements encourages thoughtful reasoning, intellectual humility, and attention to the difference between what seems true in ordinary life and what a theory claims about reality as a whole.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical practice of examining claims while holding back from deciding that one side is definitely true or false.
Choosing not to settle a question because the arguments on different sides remain balanced or unresolved.
Someone who confidently accepts a philosophical doctrine, especially one about how reality really is.
An ancient form of skepticism that uses competing arguments and avoids commitment to philosophical doctrines.
A newer form of Pyrrhonism associated in the entry with Oswaldo Porchat, who presents skepticism as a broad way of doing philosophy.
The clash between philosophical views that offer different answers to the same question.
What appears in experience or ordinary life, contrasted with theories about reality beyond what appears.

questions_to_think_about: Can a person live normally while suspending judgment about deep philosophical questions?
When does disagreement show that we need more evidence, and when does it show that the question may be hard to settle?
Why might a philosopher want to distinguish appearances from claims about reality?
Should skepticism be used only as a method, or can it be a lasting way of thinking?
